local.levelRationale: Anchored on the headline homicide rate, this dimension would score deep in safe territory alone (roughly -80): 305 murders in 2025, down 20.2% from 382 in 2024, a rate of ~3.6/100,000 — among the lowest in NYC's modern recorded history and well below the national average. But R1 requires adjusting for well-sourced shortfalls captured in the same dimension, and here they are severe, not marginal. PULLING THE LEVEL UP: (1) a federal court held the city in CONTEMPT in Nov 2024 for ongoing constitutional violations at Rikers (use-of-force, staff accountability, supervision failures); (2) the court then ordered a Remediation Manager with powers equivalent to a receiver (May 2025 order; powers detailed Dec 19, 2025; Nicholas Deml named Jan 2026) — the city has lost operational control of a core agency, an outcome with no precedent in the Nunez litigation's history; (3) in-custody deaths rebounded to 15 in 2025 from a low of 5 in 2024 (Vera Institute tracking), still below 2022's 19 but a reversal; (4) the average daily jail population (~6,747, Jan-May 2026) runs roughly 1.6-2x the 3,300-4,160 capacity the closure plan requires, and the city's own Mamdani administration has now formally acknowledged the Aug 31, 2027 legal deadline to close Rikers will be missed, with replacement jails not complete until 2029-2032; (5) 12+ years after the Floyd remedial order, NYPD accountability remains structurally weak: CCRB complaints hit a decade-high in 2024 (5,663), NYPD implements fewer than half of CCRB's substantiated non-disciplinary recommendations, and the city paid $117M-$206M/year in misconduct settlements (2024-2025); (6) stop-and-frisk racial disparities persist even as volume fell — Black drivers were 32% of NYPD's 2M+ 2024 traffic stops against ~20-23% of the city's population, and searched at roughly 9x the rate of white drivers. Net: street-level violence is a genuine, well-evidenced NYC strength; the carceral and police-accountability side of this dimension is a genuine, court-documented crisis. The two do not average to a mild score — they coexist, and the level (45, 'needs attention' tilting toward critical) is deliberately anchored closer to the carceral-system failure because it represents an active, unresolved federal constitutional violation, which this framework treats as more structurally severe than a favorable-but-improving crime trend.
local.indicator: Homicide (murder) rate per 100,000 residents, dimension-adjusted per R1 for the Rikers/NYPD-accountability sub-indicators above
local.value: 305 homicides citywide in 2025 (NYPD year-end figure), -20.2% vs 382 in 2024; rate ~3.6 per 100,000 (derived: 305 / 8,478,072 [Census Vintage 2024 NYC population estimate] x 100,000; NYPD figure, Census denominator, so labeled derived, confidence medium for the rate specifically, high for the raw count). Shooting incidents: 688 in 2025 (-24% vs 904 in 2024), also a recorded-history low. Note press variance in early tallies (302-303-309 reported before final NYPD compilation) — 305 is the figure in the joint NYPD/Governor's Office year-end release and is treated as authoritative per R11.
local.target: No single NYC statutory target for homicide rate exists; treated against a 'continued reduction toward historic lows, below the national average' standard implicit in NYPD's own CompStat framing and against the Nunez consent judgment's constitutional-minimum standard for the jail system.
local.context: NYC recorded its lowest murder total in the modern CompStat era in 2025, a genuine and heavily-verified result (multiple independent city, state, and press sources converge on ~305, -20%). This is the headline strength of the dimension. But 'peace & justice' in the Doughnut framework is not only about violence between residents — it is also about the justice system's treatment of the people it holds, and there NYC's headline number tells a starkly different story: a federal judge found the city in contempt of a 13-year-old consent judgment, then took the unprecedented step of ordering a court-appointed Remediation Manager (functionally a receiver) with hiring/firing and policy-making authority over DOC, because in-custody deaths and use-of-force incidents kept rising despite four mayoral administrations' worth of monitoring. NYC is simultaneously one of the safest large US cities on the street and running a jail system a federal court has found unconstitutional — a genuine structural tension, not a data error, and the two facts must be reported side by side rather than blended into a false middle. The policy lever for the carceral crisis is the Nunez remediation process and the borough-based jails construction timeline; the lever for street violence is continued precision-policing and Crisis Management System investment, which itself faces funding pressure (see subIndicators).
local.source: NYPD (year-end 2025 CompStat release, via NYS Governor's Office joint announcement); Vera Institute (in-custody deaths); S.D.N.Y. Nunez docket

bronx.note: Murders fell 18% in the Bronx in 2025 (NYPD/Governor's Office release, same source as citywide figure) — verified and same indicator as the headline, but no full-year absolute count could be sourced to a fetchable primary document within this research pass (the NYPD borough PDF cs-en-us-pbbx.pdf 404'd). The closest dated data point: Bronx murders YTD through Oct 26, 2025 stood at 89, down 14.4% from 104 over the same period in 2024 (Bronx Times, citing NYPD CompStat). Per R6/R10, this is left null rather than estimated from the percentage. NYPD CompStat 2.0 (compstat.nypdonline.org) would have the exact full-year count.

brooklyn.value: 91 murders in 2025, down from 120 in 2024 (-24%); derived rate ~3.48 per 100,000 (91 / 2,617,631 Kings County 2024 ACS population)
brooklyn.source: Brooklyn District Attorney's Office year-end release, via Brooklyn Eagle/amNewYork; population from U.S. Census ACS 2024 1-Year

manhattan.note: Murders fell 33% in Manhattan in 2025 (NYPD/Governor's Office release) — verified, same indicator, but no full-year absolute count was found at a fetchable primary source; the NYPD borough PDF (cs-en-us-pbmn.pdf) fetched but returned as an unreadable scanned/encoded document. Left null per R6/R10 rather than back-calculated from the percentage.

queens.value: 58 murders in 2025, up from 55 in 2024 (+7%) — the only borough where murders rose; derived rate ~2.50 per 100,000 (58 / 2,316,841 Queens County 2024 ACS population)
queens.source: Queens Chronicle, citing NYPD data; population from U.S. Census ACS 2024 1-Year

statenIsland.value: 3 murders in 2025, a recorded-history low, down more than 60% year-over-year; derived rate ~0.60 per 100,000 (3 / 498,212 Richmond County 2024 ACS population)
statenIsland.source: NYPD/Governor's Office year-end release; 2024 baseline for Staten Island not independently confirmed to an exact count within this research pass

local.neighborhoodNote: Violence remains geographically concentrated even as citywide totals fall: the Brennan Center's Nov 2025 analysis identifies the South Bronx, Brownsville (Brooklyn), and East Harlem (Manhattan) as retaining elevated shooting rates relative to the rest of the city. Precinct-level 2025 data show uneven progress even within boroughs — e.g., Brooklyn's 70th Precinct (Flatbush) posted a 28.6% major-crime decline while Queens' 115th Precinct (Jackson Heights/East Elmhurst/North Corona) saw murders rise from 4 to 7 even as overall major crime fell 23.9% there. A precise 2025 ranking of highest-violence precincts would require NYPD CompStat 2.0's own precinct tables, which are the authoritative source and were not fully machine-readable in this pass.

subIndicators.name: Rikers/DOC in-custody deaths, by year
subIndicators.value: 2022: 19 (widely reported as the deadliest year in roughly a decade); 2023: 9; 2024: 5; 2025: 15; 2026 YTD through July: 4
subIndicators.source: Vera Institute, NYC jail deaths tracker

subIndicators.name: Average daily jail population vs. planned closure capacity
subIndicators.value: ~6,747 average daily population, Jan-May 2026, against the 3,300-4,160-bed capacity of the four borough-based jails the 2019/2021 closure law requires
subIndicators.source: NYS DCJS Monthly Jail Population Trends / NYC DOC

subIndicators.name: CCRB complaint volume and discipline implementation
subIndicators.value: 5,663 complaints filed against NYPD officers in 2024, a decade-high (62% increase over two years, driven by excessive-force complaints); NYPD served charges in 86.3% of the most serious (Charges) cases but did not implement CCRB's recommended discipline in more than 50% of substantiated non-Charges cases, Jan 2024-May 2025; case substantiation rate ~39.9% (Jan 2024-June 2025)
subIndicators.source: CCRB Annual Report 2025 / NY1 reporting on CCRB data

subIndicators.name: NYPD misconduct settlement costs
subIndicators.value: $206.3M paid in 2024 (record high); $117.25M paid in 2025 across 1,044 lawsuits — the fourth consecutive year above $100M; $834.1M cumulative since 2018
subIndicators.source: NYC Comptroller Annual Claims Report data, via The Legal Aid Society's Cop Accountability Project

subIndicators.name: Traffic-violence context (correctly attributed to the mobility dimension, not peace & justice's headline)
subIndicators.value: 205 traffic deaths in 2025 — the fewest since NYC record-keeping began in 1910, down 19% YoY and 31% since 2014 (NYC DOT). Per the orchestrator's R14, this is a verified NYC strength, not a rising-violence signal, and is scored under the mobility dimension; noted here only because the research pointer for this dimension referenced it.

subIndicators.name: NYPD traffic-stop racial disparity
subIndicators.value: Of 2M+ NYPD traffic stops in 2024: Black drivers 32% of stops, Latino 30%, white 23% — against a citywide population that is ~22.7% Black, ~28.4% Hispanic, ~31.3% white (ACS). Black drivers searched at ~9x the rate of white drivers, Latino drivers at ~6x, 2022-2025.
subIndicators.source: NYCLU / New York Focus analysis of NYPD vehicle-stop data

subIndicators.name: Stop-and-frisk (Terry stop) volume and Floyd monitorship status
subIndicators.value: Over 25,000 recorded stop-and-frisks in 2024, up ~50% from ~15,000-16,000 in each of 2022 and 2023 (increase partly attributable to expanded reporting requirements under the How Many Stops Act, effective Sept 2024, not solely to more stops). A random sample of body-camera footage found 31.4% of stops undocumented, per the Floyd monitor's Feb 2025 report; NYPD submitted a revised compliance plan, including a new Racial Disparities Review Committee, on Dec 31, 2025.
subIndicators.source: NYPD Monitor (Floyd v. City of New York) reports; Center for Constitutional Rights

subIndicators.name: Hate crimes
subIndicators.value: 576 total suspected hate crimes reported in 2025, down 12% from 2024; 330 (57%) were antisemitic incidents, a 3% decrease from 339 in 2024. NYPD's Hate Crime Task Force investigates and confirms incidents; a live NYC Open Data / Power BI dashboard exists but exact current totals could not be independently pulled from it in this pass.
subIndicators.source: NYPD data, reported via Times of Israel/JNS

subIndicators.name: Bail reform status
subIndicators.value: The 2019 bail-reform law has been amended three times (2020, 2022, 2023) to expand 'qualifying offenses' where judges may set bail; as of mid-2026, multiple further amendment bills (restoring broader judicial discretion, risk-and-needs assessments) are pending in Albany but not enacted. The Brennan Center's ongoing tracking finds the law's effects on public safety and racial disparity in pretrial detention contested and evidence-mixed; this dossier does not assert a settled empirical verdict.
subIndicators.source: NYS Senate bill tracker; Brennan Center for Justice

subIndicators.name: Crisis Management System / community violence intervention
subIndicators.value: NYC's Crisis Management System (Cure Violence-model programs) is credited with contributing to a 21% reduction in gun violence, 2012-2024 (Comptroller's office analysis), but the program faces a federal funding cliff and no confirmed new city baseline expansion despite a prior mayoral pledge; NY State created a permanent Office of Gun Violence Prevention in the FY2026 state budget as a partial backstop.

subIndicators.name: B-HEARD mental-health crisis response
subIndicators.value: ~35,000 mental-health 911 calls handled by B-HEARD teams since 2021 launch through June 2025; 43% of clinically-assessed patients served in the community rather than transported to a hospital ED. A May 2025 Comptroller audit found ~14,000 eligible calls outside pilot hours went unserved, and the share diverted to community-based care fell from 10% (H2 2022) to 6% (H1 2023). Program transitioned fully to NYC Health + Hospitals in Nov 2025.
subIndicators.source: Mayor's Office of Community Mental Health; NYC Comptroller audit

subIndicators.name: FBI UCR violent crime rate (broader index than homicide)
subIndicators.value: 671 violent crimes per 100,000 in 2024 (55,690 total: 325 murders [UCR definitional count, differs slightly from NYPD's operational 377-382], 15,559 robberies, 37,863 aggravated assaults, 1,943 rapes) — 91% above the national average and 77% above the New York State average.
subIndicators.source: FBI Uniform Crime Reporting / Crime Data Explorer

global.levelRationale: Two real, quantified transmission channels exist for this dimension, pulling in opposite directions, and neither has an established benchmark or fair-share target to score severity against — so per R2, this is scored null with strong framing rather than forced into a number. (1) NYC as a destination for people fleeing conflict and persecution: more than 237,000 asylum seekers have come through the city's care since spring 2022 (city-scale, quantified, a genuine positive contribution to global displacement response, tracked against a 117.8M-person global forcibly-displaced population at end of 2025 per UNHCR). (2) NYC's financial sector as a capital allocator to the industries this dimension is concerned with: NYC's public pension funds' Palantir holdings — a firm with major ICE and defense/surveillance contracts — grew from ~$17.6M (2022) to ~$56.6M (2024), and the funds hold $1.5M+ in Elbit Systems (an Israeli arms manufacturer) as part of ~$300M in Israeli-company equities, per December 2025 disclosures. There is no accepted way to net a refugee-hosting figure against a portfolio-holdings figure into one severity score, and no external target defines how much of either NYC 'should' have. Both figures are carried here, quantified and sourced, rather than compressed into an invented level.
global.indicator: NYC as conflict-displacement destination (asylum arrivals) and as capital allocator to weapons/surveillance-linked holdings (pension fund equities) — two distinct transmission channels, not scored against each other
global.value: 237,000+ cumulative asylum seekers received into NYC's care since spring 2022 (as of July 2025 data; weekly arrivals fell from a peak of ~4,000 to under 100 by mid-2025, and the city closed its dedicated Asylum Arrival Center in 2025); NYC pension funds' Palantir Technologies holdings ~$56.6M (2024), up from ~$17.6M (2022); ~$1.5M+ in Elbit Systems and ~$300M across Israeli-company equities (Dec 2025 disclosures, reviewed via public pension records)
global.target: No established city-scale or portfolio-scale benchmark exists for either channel; UNHCR's 117.8M-person end-2025 global forcibly-displaced figure is cited as world-scale context, not a target NYC is measured against.
global.context: NYC hosts the United Nations headquarters and its annual General Assembly high-level week — the institutional home of the post-1945 international peace and security architecture — which is a qualitative fact about the city's global role in this dimension, not a quantified one. More concretely: NYC has absorbed one of the largest municipal shares of the 2022-2025 US asylum-seeker influx of any US city, a genuine (if now-declining) contribution to global displacement response that this framework can quantify. At the same time, as one of the world's largest financial centers, NYC-headquartered and NYC-pension-fund capital is allocated into companies tied to surveillance, immigration enforcement, and arms manufacturing — a transmission channel in the other direction that the same city's residents (via their pension funds) are exposed to and, through worker-led divestment campaigns since 2024, are actively contesting. The 9/11 attacks also durably reshaped NYC's own security posture (NYPD counterterrorism apparatus, hardened public infrastructure) in ways not quantified here. Whoever eventually scores this systematically would need the NYC Comptroller's SRI/stewardship team (portfolio composition) and MOIA/the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs (displacement-hosting data) working from a common framework — neither currently exists.
global.source: NYC Comptroller pension disclosures (via amNewYork/Break the Chain reporting); NYC Mayor's Office (asylum arrivals); UNHCR Mid-Year and Global Trends reports

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 192 of 2019 (Rikers closure)
policyAnchors.relevance: Mandates closing all jails on Rikers Island and replacing them with four borough-based jails (design capacity now 4,160 beds, up from an original 3,300)
policyAnchors.status2026: Legally binding Aug 31, 2027 deadline remains on the books, but the Mamdani administration formally acknowledged in Jan 2026 that it will not be met; an independent commission confirmed the same finding. Brooklyn's jail is now slated for 2029, Queens/Bronx for 2031, Manhattan for mid-2032 — up to five years past the legal deadline. Mamdani signed an emergency executive order in Jan 2026 directing DOC to produce a 45-day compliance plan; no new statutory deadline has been enacted as of this research.

policyAnchors.name: Nunez v. City of New York consent judgment and contempt/remediation order
policyAnchors.relevance: The federal consent judgment governing use of force and safety conditions in NYC jails
policyAnchors.status2026: Contempt finding issued Nov 2024 (18 provisions of 4 court orders violated); Remediation Manager appointment order granted May 13, 2025; powers detailed in a Dec 19, 2025 opinion (functionally receivership: hiring/firing/policy authority over DOC, minimum 7-year term, city bears all costs); Nicholas Deml named as Remediation Manager Jan 27, 2026, with formal appointment pending a negotiated office budget; his first status report with remediation deadlines was issued July 2026.

policyAnchors.name: Floyd v. City of New York remedial order (stop-and-frisk monitorship)
policyAnchors.relevance: The 2013 ruling finding NYPD's stop-and-frisk practice unconstitutional and racially discriminatory; established the ongoing federal monitorship
policyAnchors.status2026: Monitorship remains active 13 years on; the monitor's Feb 2025 report on Neighborhood/Public Safety Teams found continued illegal stops and profiling; NYPD's Dec 31, 2025 response plan creates a new Racial Disparities Review Committee. The 20th Monitor's Report was issued Jan 13, 2026.

policyAnchors.name: How Many Stops Act (Local Laws, 2024)
policyAnchors.relevance: Requires NYPD to report previously-unreported 'Level 1' and 'Level 2' investigative stops, not just full Terry stops
policyAnchors.status2026: Passed by City Council veto override Jan 30, 2024 (42-9), effective for reporting purposes from Sept 2024. Contributed to a documented rise in recorded stop-and-frisk volume in 2024-2025, though this is partly a reporting-transparency effect, not solely a volume increase.

policyAnchors.name: Bail Reform Act (2019, amended 2020/2022/2023)
policyAnchors.relevance: Governs which offenses are bail-eligible and under what standard
policyAnchors.status2026: Current law separates offenses into mandatory-release, judicial-discretion (qualifying), and remand-eligible categories; three rounds of amendments since 2019 have expanded qualifying offenses. Multiple further amendment bills are pending in the NYS Legislature as of mid-2026 but not enacted.

actions: Monitor the Nunez Remediation Manager's public status reports and deadlines via the NYC Board of Correction (nyc.gov/boc) and nypdmonitor.org.
Track NYPD's Level 1/2 stop data now published under the How Many Stops Act via NYC Open Data, and press City Council oversight hearings on the Racial Disparities Review Committee's findings.
File complaints and track case outcomes through the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB), and follow its Annual Report for NYPD's discipline-implementation rate.

Support restoration of Crisis Management System / Cure Violence funding through the Legal Aid Society's Community Justice Unit and advocate for the state's new Office of Gun Violence Prevention to backstop lost federal funds.
Push for B-HEARD's expansion (hours, geography, eligible call types) as it transitions fully to NYC Health + Hospitals, per the Comptroller's May 2025 audit findings.
Engage NYCERS/other NYC pension trustee board meetings on the worker-led divestment campaign targeting Israeli-linked and defense/surveillance holdings (e.g., Palantir, Elbit Systems).
petalumaContrast: Petaluma's peace & justice indicator is violent crime rate: 510.7 per 100,000 (2023, FBI/Petaluma PD), essentially tied with the California state average, scored at level 30. NYC's FBI-defined violent crime rate is actually higher — 671 per 100,000 (2024) — even though NYC's homicide rate (~3.6/100,000) is far lower than a naive city-size comparison would predict and is near modern-era lows. The two portraits also diverge structurally, not just numerically: Petaluma has no jail system of its own comparable to Rikers and no analog to a federal consent-judgment/receivership crisis — NYC's carceral-system failure is a scale-specific phenomenon a small city like Petaluma simply does not have the apparatus to produce, which is why this dossier scores NYC's dimension level (45) well above what its street-crime data alone would suggest.

questionsForOrchestrator: Is 'homicide rate' the right sole headline indicator for this dimension given R1, or should the schema support a genuinely dual headline (e.g., 'homicide rate' + 'Rikers constitutional-compliance status') so the local.value field doesn't have to carry both a rate and a receivership narrative in prose? The current single-indicator/adjusted-level structure works but is doing a lot of work in levelRationale.

For the global lens, is it acceptable to leave level null when I have two real, quantified, but non-commensurable transmission channels (asylum hosting vs. pension-fund weapons/surveillance holdings), or would the orchestrator prefer a directional-only level (e.g., a modest negative number reflecting that hosting displaced people net-positively outweighs the portfolio exposure) even without a formal benchmark?

Should FBI UCR violent crime rate (671/100k, 2024) or NYPD's own homicide-specific figure be the dimension's primary cross-portrait comparison point in petalumaContrast, given that Petaluma's own indicator (510.7/100k) is a UCR violent-crime rate, not a homicide rate?
